subject: Medieval History
sub_topic: Akbar's revenue system — Zabt system under Todar Mal

concepts.name: Zabt System: Definition, Scope, and Geographical Applicability
key_dimensions: Definition of 'Zabt' (measurement-based assessment) versus other revenue methods
Geographical limitation — applied primarily to areas where Akbar personally campaigned (Punjab, UP, Agra, Malwa, Gujarat) and NOT uniformly across the empire
UPSC trap: Zabt was NOT a pan-empire system — Bengal, Deccan, Kabul used different methods
Distinction between Zabt as a system versus Ain-i-Dahsala as its refined 10-year average mechanism

concepts.name: Todar Mal: Role, Career Trajectory, and Institutional Contribution
key_dimensions: Todar Mal's service under Sher Shah Suri before joining Akbar — continuity of revenue ideas
Appointment as Diwan (revenue minister) and later as Wazir under Akbar
His role in standardizing land measurement, revenue records, and cadastral surveys
UPSC trap: Todar Mal refined and systematized an existing framework rather than inventing it from scratch — Sher Shah's earlier surveys were a precursor

concepts.name: Ain-i-Dahsala (Ten-Year Average System): Mechanism and Significance
key_dimensions: Collection of crop prices and yield data over 10 years (1571–1580) to calculate average demand
Revenue fixed in cash (daam) based on average productivity — reduced annual fluctuation burden on peasants
Difference between Ain-i-Dahsala (pricing/averaging mechanism) and Zabt (measurement/survey mechanism) — often conflated in questions
Significance: provided stability, predictability, and rationalization of state demand

concepts.name: Land Measurement and Survey Operations under Todar Mal
key_dimensions: Introduction of standardized Ilahi gaz (yard) for uniform land measurement across the empire
Use of bamboo rods with iron rings (jarib) replacing unreliable hemp ropes for accurate survey
Classification of land into four categories: Polaj, Parauti, Chachar, Banjar — based on cultivation frequency
UPSC trap: The four-fold land classification is often confused with crop classification (Kharif, Rabi, Zaid)

concepts.name: Land Classification System: Polaj, Parauti, Chachar, Banjar
key_dimensions: Polaj — land under annual cultivation, highest revenue assessment
Parauti — land left fallow for one or two years to recover fertility, assessed at reduced rate
Chachar — land uncultivated for 3–4 years, further reduced assessment
Banjar — long-fallow (5+ years) land, lowest or no assessment; incentive structure embedded in classification
UPSC trap: Banjar Old vs Banjar New distinction and how revenue exemptions worked as agricultural incentives

concepts.name: Crop Classification: Kharif, Rabi, and Zaid under the Zabt System
key_dimensions: Separate schedules (dasturs) maintained for Kharif (summer) and Rabi (winter) crops
State demand varied crop-to-crop — cash crops like sugarcane and cotton assessed at higher rates
Zaid (intermediate/spring crops) and their revenue treatment
Significance of crop-specific assessment in making the system more equitable than flat-rate systems

concepts.name: Dastur-ul-Amal: Provincial Revenue Schedules and Rate Fixation
key_dimensions: Dastur (schedule of rates) compiled for each pargana based on local prices and productivity
State demand fixed at approximately 1/3rd of estimated produce under Akbar (compared to Alauddin Khalji's 50% or Sher Shah's varying rates)
Variation of dasturs by region — reflecting price differences across the empire
UPSC trap: The '1/3rd demand' rule was normative, not always followed uniformly; Bernier and other travellers noted heavier actual burdens

concepts.name: Sher Shah Suri's Revenue Legacy and Continuity into the Zabt System
key_dimensions: Sher Shah introduced pattas (title deeds to peasants) and qabuliyats (peasant agreements) — continued under Akbar
Sher Shah's cadastral surveys and per-bigha rates as direct predecessor to Todar Mal's reforms
Akbar-Todar Mal's contribution: systematization, standardization, and extension of Sher Shah's framework
UPSC trap: Crediting Akbar alone for the Zabt system without acknowledging Sher Shah's foundational work

concepts.name: Patta and Qabuliyat System under Akbar
key_dimensions: Patta: formal written document issued to peasant specifying the land held and revenue due
Qabuliyat: peasant's written acceptance of the revenue demand — created a contractual relationship
Significance: introduced legal accountability and reduced arbitrary exaction by zamindars and local officials
UPSC trap: Patta-Qabuliyat system is often associated with Sher Shah but was institutionalized under Akbar's administration

concepts.name: Role of Amil, Qanungo, and Patwari in Revenue Administration
key_dimensions: Amil: revenue collector at the pargana level responsible for assessment and collection
Qanungo: hereditary local accountant who maintained land records — intermediary between state and peasant
Patwari: village-level accountant maintaining crop and revenue registers (khasra, khatauni)
UPSC trap: Confusion between the hierarchical roles — Qanungo vs Patwari vs Amil as distinct functionaries

concepts.name: Mansabdari System's Relationship with the Zabt Revenue System
key_dimensions: Mansabdars paid in cash (naqd) or assigned jagirs — jagir areas subject to Zabt assessment provided the revenue base
Tension between jagirdari system and centralized Zabt: jagirdars had incentive to extract beyond Zabt rates
Akbar's attempt to maintain Khalisa (crown land) assessed under Zabt as a check on jagirdari extraction
UPSC trap: Zabt system applied to both Khalisa and jagir lands in theory, but enforcement differed significantly

concepts.name: Khalisa vs Jagir Lands: Revenue Collection Differences
key_dimensions: Khalisa: crown land whose revenue went directly to the imperial treasury — Zabt most strictly applied here
Jagir: revenue assignment to mansabdars — Zabt provided the benchmark but actual collection often exceeded it
Akbar's policy of expanding Khalisa as a fiscal stabilization strategy
UPSC trap: Akbar is often credited with reducing jagir lands, but the balance between Khalisa and jagir shifted repeatedly across his reign

concepts.name: Cash vs Kind Revenue Payment: Shift under the Zabt System
key_dimensions: Zabt system monetized revenue demand — payment in cash (daam, rupee) preferred over payment in kind
Significance: stimulated market economy, monetization, and peasant integration into cash economy
Practical challenge: peasants had to sell produce to pay cash — made them vulnerable to market price fluctuations
UPSC trap: The shift to cash was not absolute — batai (crop-sharing) and kankut (estimation) methods continued in non-Zabt areas

concepts.name: Batai, Kankut, and Nasaq: Alternative Revenue Systems Coexisting with Zabt
key_dimensions: Batai (crop-sharing): actual division of harvest between state and peasant — 1/3 or 1/2 to state
Kankut (estimate): visual/crop-cutting estimate of standing crop yield, used where measurement impractical
Nasaq: customary assessment based on past records without fresh measurement — common in difficult terrain
UPSC trap: Multiple systems coexisted — UPSC may ask which system applied where, or compare their merits/demerits

concepts.name: Ain-i-Akbari as a Source for Understanding the Zabt System
key_dimensions: Abul Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari (part of Akbarnama) contains detailed revenue statistics, dastur schedules, and administrative rules
Ain-i-Akbari as a primary source: its strengths (administrative detail) and limitations (official/eulogistic bias)
Revenue data in Ain-i-Akbari used by historians like Irfan Habib to reconstruct agrarian history
UPSC trap: Ain-i-Akbari is sometimes confused with Akbarnama as a whole — Ain is the third volume dealing with administration

concepts.name: Irfan Habib's Agrarian System of the Mughal Empire: Historiographical Significance
key_dimensions: Irfan Habib's thesis: Zabt system led to peasant exploitation and was a structural cause of the 17th-century agrarian crisis
Debate: Was the Zabt system progressive (rationalization) or exploitative (monetized extraction)?
Contrast with W.H. Moreland's earlier view emphasizing administrative efficiency
UPSC relevance: historiographical debates appear in GS1 and optional papers — understanding both sides is essential

concepts.name: Impact of Zabt System on Peasantry and Agrarian Economy
key_dimensions: Positive: security of tenure (through pattas), standardized demand, reduced arbitrary local exaction
Negative: cash demand forced market dependence, heavy burden during famines when rates were not revised
Role of the system in encouraging extension of cultivation (Polaj incentive) vs. its failure during droughts
UPSC trap: Akbar's reign is often romanticized — questions may probe whether the Zabt system actually benefited peasants

concepts.name: Todar Mal's Bandobast (Grand Settlement) of 1580–1582
key_dimensions: The comprehensive revenue settlement implemented after the completion of 10-year data collection (Ain-i-Dahsala)
Systematic compilation of revenue demand province-by-province — considered the high point of Mughal revenue administration
Significance: provided a stable fiscal base for Akbar's military campaigns and court expenditure
UPSC trap: 'Todar Mal's Bandobast' is sometimes used loosely — questions may test the specific timeline (1580–82) and its distinction from earlier partial surveys

concepts.name: Revenue System Comparison: Akbar's Zabt vs. Alauddin Khalji's Market Reforms vs. Sher Shah's System
key_dimensions: Alauddin: fixed prices and centralized control — coercive, no land measurement component
Sher Shah: introduced measurement and per-bigha rates but lacked 10-year averaging and systematic standardization
Akbar-Todar Mal: measurement + averaging + monetization + documentation — most systematic pre-British land revenue system
UPSC trap: Comparative questions frequently appear — knowing what was UNIQUE to each ruler's system is critical

concepts.name: Decline and Limitations of the Zabt System in Post-Akbar Period
key_dimensions: Jagirdari crisis of the 17th century: rapid rotation of jagirs prevented long-term investment, undermining Zabt's effectiveness
Failure to revise dastur rates despite inflation — real burden on peasants increased over time
Aurangzeb's reign: re-imposition of jizya and expansion of wars strained revenue system, leading to breakdown
UPSC trap: The decline of the Zabt system is linked to the broader question of why the Mughal Empire declined — a frequently asked analytical question
